title: Kernel capacity safeguards and quality delegation playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the capacity safeguard and quality delegation mechanisms the runtime scheduler uses to preserve customer SLOs while minimizing cost. It is intended for runtime engineers, on-call SREs, and product owners responsible for routing and tiering policies. The document covers design intent, concrete admission-control configurations, emergency mitigation steps for spikes and noisy tenants, and a test matrix for rollout validation.

Goals and scope
----------------
- Preserve 95th/99th latency SLOs for paid tiers under bursty traffic.
- Minimize unnecessary fidelity drops for important customers while enforcing cost controls.
- Provide clear runbook actions for incidents related to slot exhaustion, prolonged degradation, and cross-tenant interference.
- Apply to hosted, dedicated, and private modes (differences noted).

Terminology
-----------
- Slot: logical GPU time window available to a request; unit used by admission controller.
- Fidelity: an abstraction combining model variant (e.g., base/quantized/ distilled), token budgeting, and sampling temperature.
- Quality delegation: controlled, policy-driven decision to lower fidelity for non-critical traffic to preserve SLOs for higher-tier traffic.
- Safeguard pool: reserved slots (percentage of cluster) kept aside for high-priority traffic and emergency backfills.

Design overview
---------------
1) Two-tier slot accounting
   - Fast path slots: low-latency, prewarmed kernels with KV cache affinity. Targets 1–2 GPU hops.
   - Bulk slots: high-throughput, higher-latency buckets for best-effort work (large batches, background embedding jobs).

2) Safeguard pool and soft-reservation
   - Default: 8% of capacity marked as safeguard pool cluster-wide. This is configurable by offering and region.
   - Soft-reservation semantics: safeguard pool drains preferentially to fast-path requests when utilization > 92%.

3) Quality delegation policy engine
   - Decision inputs: request_priority, customer_tier, model_variant_cost, current_latency_headroom, recent_error_rate, KV_cache_hit_rate.
   - Delegation actions: model downgrade (e.g., 8-bit quantized variant), reduce max_output_tokens, switch to cached-prefix generation, or return synthetic fallback.

Configuration examples
----------------------
Below is a representative admission controller policy (YAML). Use the runtime CLI to push to the cluster: `redwoodctl scheduler apply -f policy.yaml`

YAML example:

---
policy_name: cost-aware-quality-delegation-v1
defaults:
  safeguard_percent: 8
  fast_path_threshold: 0.92   # fraction of fast-path capacity
  bulk_slot_backoff: 0.65
rules:
  - name: premium-preserve
    match:
      customer_tier: premium
    action:
      reserve_from_safeguard: 0.5   # allow premium to consume half of safeguard if needed
      max_fidelity_drop: 0.0       # do not downgrade fidelity for premium
  - name: general-peak-control
    match:
      customer_tier: standard
    action:
      max_fidelity_drop: 0.5       # allow downgrades up to 50% perceived quality
      fallback_variant_sequence: ["quantized-v2","distilled-v1"]
      token_cut_percent: 20
  - name: background-bulk
    match:
      route_tag: background
    action:
      route_to: bulk_slots
      batch_preference: true
      max_latency_slo: 2000
---

Operational thresholds and SLO mapping
-------------------------------------
- Cluster-wide fast-path utilization alarm: > 88% sustained for 2 minutes -> evaluate safeguard pressure.
- Safeguard depletion alarm: safeguard consumption > 75% -> trigger pre-emptive quality delegation for non-premium tiers.
- Customer-level degradation target: keep premium 99th latency < 600ms; standard 95th < 1.5s.
- Eviction aggressiveness scale (0–10): default 4. Increase to 7 when KV cache miss rate > 40% and fast-path latency > 90th historical.

Runbook: fast-path slot exhaustion
----------------------------------
Detection signals (automated):
1) fast_path_util >= 0.9 for 90s
2) per-model 99th latency crossing threshold
3) safeguard pool usage > 0.75
4) sustained increase in preemption events

Immediate mitigation steps (SRE primary)
1) Verify signals in the Scheduler dashboard and correlate with tracing: services/scheduler -> cluster/slots -> traces.
2) If safeguard pool is near exhausted, set a temporary override: `redwoodctl scheduler patch --set=policy.defaults.safeguard_percent=12` (will persist to audit log).
3) Enable aggressive quality delegation for standard tier: `redwoodctl policy apply --name=cost-aware-quality-delegation-v1 --override=general-peak-control.max_fidelity_drop=0.7`
4) If preemptions spike, throttle new long-running requests: `redwoodctl admission throttle --route-pattern="/v1/generate" --window=30s --max-inflight=150`
5) Notify product/support channels with incident tag: `#runtime-incident` and include the following fields: cluster, region, safeguard_usage, top-3 tenants by slot consumption.

Escalation (within 10 minutes if no improvement)
- Team: Runtime Pager -> MTL (Multi-tenant lead) -> Oncall infra.
- Action: shift best-effort background jobs to bulk_slots forcibly: `redwoodctl route set --tag=background --dest=bulk_slots`

Post-incident recovery
---------------------
1) Gradually revert temporary overrides after 15 minutes of stable fast_path_util < 0.7. Use canary revert: revert 20% of changes every 5 minutes.
2) Run the incident analysis job: `scripts/slot-usage-histogram.sh --window=1h` and upload to /incidents/<id>/artifacts.
3) Create follow-up work item if safeguards were insufficient: add to scheduler backlog with priority P1 if premium latency violated SLO.

Testing and rollout matrix
-------------------------
- Unit tests: policy engine rule evaluation table with 1000 synthetic requests.
- Integration tests: simulate 3x spike with mixed tiers; verify premium 99th < 600ms in 95% of runs.
- Chaos tests: simulate KV cache partial outage and confirm eviction aggressiveness moves to >=7 and fallback config triggers.
- Canary rollout: deploy policy to single region, run two-hour soak while monitoring: fast_path_util, safeguard_usage, premium_99p, standard_95p.

Representative simulation commands
----------------------------------
# Local load generator (example)
./tools/loadgen --cluster staging-eu --mix=30:70 --premium_qps=200 --standard_qps=300 --background_qps=100 --duration=15m

# Collect metrics after test
redwoodctl metrics query --cluster staging-eu --metric=fast_path_util --start=-20m | tee fast_path_util.csv

Quality metrics to track (dashboard prescriptive)
-----------------------------------------------
- premium_99p_latency_ms (goal < 600)
- standard_95p_latency_ms (goal < 1500)
- safeguard_percent_consumed (goal < 0.75)
- model_variant_switch_rate (goal < 0.05/min)
- failed_fidelity_delegations (count where delegation aborted due to model incompatibility)

Private and Dedicated deployment differences
-------------------------------------------
- Private: customer-managed KMS and audit policy require that any automatic downgrade to a different model_variant be explicitly logged and reversible. Policy must be shipped to the customer control plane as `policy-shim.yaml`.
- Dedicated: default safeguard_percent is negotiated in the contract and reflected in the runtime config (`contract.safeguard_percent`). Administrative override requires CA-signed approval in the audit log.

Known caveats and hard edges
---------------------------
- Cross-variant token accounting: downgrading to a quantized variant changes per-token CPU/GPU cost; heuristic cost estimates may underreport when sequence length variance is high. Monitor `per_token_energy_estimate` and adjust policy parameters.
- Fairness vs. latency: aggressive safeguard borrowing by premium customers can starve standard customers during sustained high-utilization windows. Use `reserve_from_safeguard` carefully and monitor per-tenant fairness index.
- Cold KV cache effects: policy may erroneously downgrade traffic that would have been fast-path after a warmup. Consider a short probation window (30s) where newly warmed sessions get temporary protection.

Operational play examples (CLI snippets)
--------------------------------------
# Increase safeguard to 12% in region us-west-2 for 30 minutes
redwoodctl scheduler patch --region=us-west-2 --set=policy.defaults.safeguard_percent=12 --ttl=30m

# Force route background jobs to bulk slots
redwoodctl route set --region=global --tag=background --dest=bulk_slots --reason="incident-mitigation"

# Temporarily raise eviction aggressiveness
redwoodctl scheduler patch --set=policy.defaults.eviction_aggressiveness=7 --note="KV cache miss spike"

Change history and audit guidance
--------------------------------
- All policy changes must be codified in the policy repo and reference a changelist: `policies/scheduler/*.yaml` with a linked PR.
- Short-term overrides must be applied with `--note` and `--ttl` so the audit service automatically expires them. Long-term changes must go through config review and performance testing.

Appendix A: Test scenarios and acceptance criteria
--------------------------------------------------
- Scenario A: 2.5x premium spike for 10 minutes with standard baseline unchanged -> acceptance: premium_99p stays < 600ms, standard_95p may increase up to 2s but not exceed 2.5s.
- Scenario B: KV cache cold-start during 30-minute peak -> acceptance: quality delegation triggers within 45s and reduces expensive kernel invocations by at least 30%.
- Scenario C: sustained mixed noise (top 5 tenants consuming > 60% of slots) -> acceptance: scheduler must identify noisy tenants and apply soft-rate-limits within 5 minutes, with documented rationale in incident ticket.

Appendix B: Example observability panels to include in dashboard
---------------------------------------------------------------
- Cluster: fast_path_utilization, safeguard_consumption, eviction_rate, preemption_events/min
- Tenant: slot_consumption_by_tenant (top 50), tenant_fidelity_switches/min, tenant_99p_latency
- Kernel: kernel_queue_length_by_priority, average_kernel_hold_time_ms

Appendix C: Frequently asked operational questions
--------------------------------------------------
Q: What do we do if a private deployment customer forbids automatic fidelity downgrades?
A: Ship a differentiated policy-shim that only performs non-destructive throttles (token caps and batch delays). Document the trade-offs and surface them in the onboarding questionnaire.

Q: How long should temporary overrides remain active?
A: Default TTL is 30 minutes. If the override is still required after TTL expiry, a documented manual re-approval with justification should be required (create a ticket and attach logs).
